claim: SARS-CoV-2 infection and viral entry crucially depends on the binding of its Spike protein to angiotensin converting enzyme 2 (ACE2) presented on host cells.
source: Infection and viral entry of SARS-CoV-2 crucially depends on the binding of its Spike protein to angiotensin converting enzyme 2 (ACE2) presented on host cells.
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to published literature (Wu et al., 2020; Zhou et al., 2020) as indicated in the Introduction section.

claim: Glycosylation of both Spike and ACE2 proteins is critical for their interaction.
source: Glycosylation of both proteins is critical for this interaction.
evidence: This claim is stated in the abstract and is supported by the experimental data and simulations presented throughout the manuscript.

claim: Recombinant soluble human ACE2 can neutralize SARS-CoV-2.
source: Recombinant soluble human ACE2 can neutralize SARS-CoV-2 and is currently undergoing clinical tests for the treatment of COVID-19.
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work (Monteil et al., 2020, Monteil et al., 2021) and reference to clinical trials.

claim: Engineering of ACE2 N-glycosylation by site-directed mutagenesis or glycosidase treatment resulted in enhanced binding affinities to Spike.
source: Engineering of ACE2 N-glycosylation by site-directed mutagenesis or glycosidase treatment resulted in enhanced binding affinities and improved virus neutralization without notable deleterious effects on the structural stability and catalytic activity of the protein.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from BLI measurements (Figure 6) and virus neutralization assays (Figure 7).

claim: Engineering of ACE2 N-glycosylation resulted in improved virus neutralization.
source: Engineering of ACE2 N-glycosylation by site-directed mutagenesis or glycosidase treatment resulted in enhanced binding affinities and improved virus neutralization without notable deleterious effects on the structural stability and catalytic activity of the protein.
evidence: This is supported by virus neutralization assays shown in Figure 7 and Figure 8.

claim: Engineering of ACE2 N-glycosylation did not cause notable deleterious effects on the structural stability of the protein.
source: Engineering of ACE2 N-glycosylation by site-directed mutagenesis or glycosidase treatment resulted in enhanced binding affinities and improved virus neutralization without notable deleterious effects on the structural stability and catalytic activity of the protein.
evidence: This is supported by DSC measurements shown in Figure 5.

claim: Engineering of ACE2 N-glycosylation did not cause notable deleterious effects on the catalytic activity of the protein.
source: Engineering of ACE2 N-glycosylation by site-directed mutagenesis or glycosidase treatment resulted in enhanced binding affinities and improved virus neutralization without notable deleterious effects on the structural stability and catalytic activity of the protein.
evidence: This is supported by enzymatic activity assays shown in Figures 9 and 10.

claim: Simultaneous removal of all accessible N-glycans from recombinant soluble human ACE2 yields a superior SARS-CoV-2 decoy receptor.
source: Importantly, simultaneous removal of all accessible N-glycans from recombinant soluble human ACE2 yields a superior SARS-CoV-2 decoy receptor with promise as effective treatment for COVID-19 patients.
evidence: This is supported by binding affinity data (Figure 6b) and neutralization assays (Figure 8) showing improved performance of deglyco-rshACE2.

claim: The SARS-CoV-2 Spike protein is heavily glycosylated with both complex and oligo-mannosidic type N-glycans.
source: The SARS-CoV-2 Spike protein is heavily glycosylated with both complex and oligo-mannosidic type N-glycans (Zhu et al., 2020, Hoffmann et al., 2021; Watanabe et al., 2020; Zhao et al., 2020), thereby shielding a large portion of the protein surface (Casalino et al., 2020; Sikora et al., 2021; Zimmerman et al., 2021).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to published glycoproteomic studies.

claim: Spike glycans shield a large portion of the protein surface.
source: The SARS-CoV-2 Spike protein is heavily glycosylated with both complex and oligo-mannosidic type N-glycans (Zhu et al., 2020, Hoffmann et al., 2021; Watanabe et al., 2020; Zhao et al., 2020), thereby shielding a large portion of the protein surface (Casalino et al., 2020; Sikora et al., 2021; Zimmerman et al., 2021).
evidence: This is supported by citations and confirmed by the authors' own SASA calculations showing glycans shield about 38% of the Spike protein surface.

claim: ACE2 is a glycoprotein with up to seven highly utilized sites of N-glycosylation.
source: Similarly, ACE2 is a glycoprotein with up to seven highly utilized sites of N-glycosylation (Zhao et al., 2020).
evidence: This is supported by a citation and confirmed by the authors' own glycoproteomic analysis (Figure 1—figure supplement 1).

claim: Glycans at N122, N165, and N343 on Spike directly interact with ACE2 or its glycans.
source: Further analysis showed that glycans at N122, N165, and N343 on Spike directly interact with ACE2 or its glycans (Figures 1b, c, 2b and c).
evidence: This is supported by molecular dynamics simulation data shown in Figures 1 and 2.

claim: Spike mutants lacking the glycans at N331 and N343 display reduced infectivity.
source: It has been reported that Spike mutants lacking the glycans at N331 and N343 display reduced infectivity, while elimination of the glycosylation motif at N234 results in increased resistance to neutralizing antibodies, without reducing infectivity of the virus (Li et al., 2020).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to published work (Li et al., 2020).

claim: Elimination of the glycosylation motif at N234 results in increased resistance to neutralizing antibodies, without reducing infectivity of the virus.
source: It has been reported that Spike mutants lacking the glycans at N331 and N343 display reduced infectivity, while elimination of the glycosylation motif at N234 results in increased resistance to neutralizing antibodies, without reducing infectivity of the virus (Li et al., 2020).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to published work (Li et al., 2020).

claim: Removing the glycans at N165, N234 and N343 was experimentally seen to reduce binding to ACE2 by 10%, 40%, and 56%, respectively.
source: Removing the glycans at N165, N234 and N343 was experimentally seen to reduce binding to ACE2 by 10%, 40%, and 56%, respectively (Casalino et al., 2020; Sztain et al., 2021).
evidence: This is supported by citations to published experimental work (Casalino et al., 2020; Sztain et al., 2021).

claim: The glycan at position N343 interacts directly with ACE2.
source: In our MD simulations, the glycan at position N343 interacts directly with ACE2 (Figure 2), while the glycan at N331 interacts with a neighboring Spike monomer (Figure 1c, Figure 2—figure supplement 2), indicating that the N331 glycosylation site only indirectly affects the interaction of Spike with ACE2.
evidence: This is supported by molecular dynamics simulation data shown in Figure 2.

claim: The glycan at N331 interacts with a neighboring Spike monomer.
source: In our MD simulations, the glycan at position N343 interacts directly with ACE2 (Figure 2), while the glycan at N331 interacts with a neighboring Spike monomer (Figure 1c, Figure 2—figure supplement 2), indicating that the N331 glycosylation site only indirectly affects the interaction of Spike with ACE2.
evidence: This is supported by molecular dynamics simulation data shown in Figure 1c and Figure 2—figure supplement 2.

claim: The N331 glycosylation site only indirectly affects the interaction of Spike with ACE2.
source: In our MD simulations, the glycan at position N343 interacts directly with ACE2 (Figure 2), while the glycan at N331 interacts with a neighboring Spike monomer (Figure 1c, Figure 2—figure supplement 2), indicating that the N331 glycosylation site only indirectly affects the interaction of Spike with ACE2.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the MD simulation data showing N331 glycan interactions with neighboring Spike monomers rather than ACE2.

claim: The glycan at N234 does not interact directly with ACE2, but seems to stabilize the 'up' conformation.
source: In our model, the glycan at N234 also does not interact directly with ACE2, but seems to stabilize the 'up' conformation.
evidence: This is based on inference from the MD simulation data and structural analysis.

claim: The Man9 glycan at N234 of Spike partially inserts itself into the vacant space in the core of the trimer that is created when the RBD of monomer three is in the 'up' conformation.
source: In agreement with previous simulations (Casalino et al., 2020) the Man9 glycan at N234 of Spike partially inserts itself into the vacant space in the core of the trimer that is created when the RBD of monomer three is in the 'up' conformation (Figure 1—figure supplement 4).
evidence: This is supported by MD simulation data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 4 and corroborated by citation to previous work (Casalino et al., 2020).

claim: Binding to ACE2 has a stabilizing effect on the Spike monomer.
source: In our simulations, the free space created by the 'up' conformation seems slightly smaller for Spike in complex with ACE2, suggesting that binding to ACE2 has a stabilizing effect on the Spike monomer.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the MD simulation observations.

claim: The N165Q mutant was experimentally found to be more sensitive to neutralization.
source: The N165Q mutant was experimentally found to be more sensitive to neutralization (Li et al., 2020).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to published experimental work (Li et al., 2020).

claim: The glycan at N165 is positioned directly next to the RBD and thus could shield important antigenic sites.
source: In our models, the glycan at N165 is positioned directly next to the RBD (Figure 1b) and thus could shield important antigenic sites.
evidence: This is based on structural analysis from the MD simulations shown in Figure 1b.

claim: Glycans account for up to 51% of the Spike-ACE2 interface area.
source: The total interface area was 24.6 nm², with glycans accounting for up to 51% of the interface area, that is 12.6 nm², contributed by the four most relevant glycans at positions N53, N90, N322, and N546 of ACE2 (Figure 3).
evidence: This is based on SASA calculations from MD simulations shown in Figure 3.

claim: The four most relevant glycans at positions N53, N90, N322, and N546 of ACE2 contribute 12.6 nm² to the interface area.
source: The total interface area was 24.6 nm², with glycans accounting for up to 51% of the interface area, that is 12.6 nm², contributed by the four most relevant glycans at positions N53, N90, N322, and N546 of ACE2 (Figure 3).
evidence: This is based on SASA calculations from MD simulations shown in Figure 3.

claim: The glycans at N53, N90, N322, and N546 interact with Spike.
source: Furthermore, we scored the number of atoms of each ACE2 glycan in contact with Spike. A contact was defined as a distance of less than 0.4 nm between two atoms. This allowed us to identify the glycans at N53, N90, N322, and N546 as interacting with Spike, with the glycan at position N53 having the weakest interaction.
evidence: This is based on contact analysis from MD simulations shown in Figure 3.

claim: The glycan at position N53 has the weakest interaction with Spike among the four interacting glycans.
source: This allowed us to identify the glycans at N53, N90, N322, and N546 as interacting with Spike, with the glycan at position N53 having the weakest interaction.
evidence: This is based on contact analysis from MD simulations shown in Figure 3.

claim: The glycans at N90 and N322 interact directly with Spike protein atoms.
source: Interestingly, the glycans at N90 and N322 interact directly with Spike protein atoms, while the glycan at N546 (red sticks in Figure 1f) interacts with the glycans at N122 and N165 of Spike (dark green and orange sticks in Figure 1b).
evidence: This is based on analysis of MD simulation data shown in Figures 1 and 3.

claim: The glycan at N546 interacts with the glycans at N122 and N165 of Spike.
source: Interestingly, the glycans at N90 and N322 interact directly with Spike protein atoms, while the glycan at N546 (red sticks in Figure 1f) interacts with the glycans at N122 and N165 of Spike (dark green and orange sticks in Figure 1b).
evidence: This is based on analysis of MD simulation data shown in Figures 1 and 3.

claim: A single glycan at N90 is observed to form up to 30 hydrogen bonds to Spike.
source: A single glycan at N90 is observed to form up to 30 hydrogen bonds to Spike and to be responsible for an interface area of up to 10 nm2, representing almost 40% of the average total interface area between Spike and ACE2.
evidence: This is based on hydrogen bond and interface area analysis from MD simulations shown in Figure 3.

claim: A single glycan at N90 is responsible for an interface area of up to 10 nm2, representing almost 40% of the average total interface area between Spike and ACE2.
source: A single glycan at N90 is observed to form up to 30 hydrogen bonds to Spike and to be responsible for an interface area of up to 10 nm2, representing almost 40% of the average total interface area between Spike and ACE2.
evidence: This is based on interface area analysis from MD simulations shown in Figure 3.

claim: Formation of the ACE2-Spike complex significantly reduces the conformational freedom of the glycans, in particular the ones at N90 and N322.
source: Formation of the ACE2-Spike complex significantly reduces the conformational freedom of the glycans, in particular the ones at N90 and N322 (Figure 4b).
evidence: This is based on density map analysis from MD simulations shown in Figure 4.

claim: The glycans at N90 and N322 hamper binding to Spike, either sterically or through an entropic penalty upon binding due to a loss of conformational freedom.
source: We predict that the glycans at N90 and N322 hamper binding to Spike, either sterically or through an entropic penalty upon binding due to a loss of conformational freedom.
evidence: This is a prediction based on the conformational analysis from MD simulations shown in Figure 4.

claim: The Tm1 midpoint transition temperatures of the ACE2-Fc glycomutants (53.3°C–54.0°C) were slightly higher than for the wild-type protein (52.2 °C).
source: The Tm1 midpoint transition temperatures of the ACE2-Fc glycomutants (53.3°C–54.0°C) were slightly higher than for the wild-type protein (52.2 °C), while Tm2 and Tm3 remained unchanged (Figure 5).
evidence: This is based on DSC measurements shown in Figure 5.

claim: Removal of the N90 and N322 glycans does not compromise the structural integrity of ACE2.
source: This indicates that removal of the N90 and N322 glycans does not compromise the structural integrity of ACE2.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the DSC data showing maintained or improved thermal stability (Figure 5).

claim: The removal of protein N-glycosylation at either N90 or N322 results in up to twofold higher binding affinities to RBD, when compared to ACE2-wt-Fc.
source: The BLI data are in good agreement with our computational models, confirming that the removal of protein N-glycosylation at either N90 or N322 results in up to twofold higher binding affinities, when compared to ACE2-wt-Fc (ACE2-wt-Fc: KD = 16.2 ± 0.7 nM; ACE2-T92Q-Fc: KD = 8.0 ± 0.7 nM; ACE2-N322Q-Fc: KD = 11.4 ± 0.3 nM; Figure 6b; Figure 6—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is based on BLI measurements shown in Figure 6b and Figure 6—figure supplement 2.

claim: ACE2-T92Q-Fc has a KD of 8.0 ± 0.7 nM for RBD binding.
source: The BLI data are in good agreement with our computational models, confirming that the removal of protein N-glycosylation at either N90 or N322 results in up to twofold higher binding affinities, when compared to ACE2-wt-Fc (ACE2-wt-Fc: KD = 16.2 ± 0.7 nM; ACE2-T92Q-Fc: KD = 8.0 ± 0.7 nM; ACE2-N322Q-Fc: KD = 11.4 ± 0.3 nM; Figure 6b; Figure 6—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is based on BLI measurements shown in Figure 6b.

claim: ACE2-N322Q-Fc has a KD of 11.4 ± 0.3 nM for RBD binding.
source: The BLI data are in good agreement with our computational models, confirming that the removal of protein N-glycosylation at either N90 or N322 results in up to twofold higher binding affinities, when compared to ACE2-wt-Fc (ACE2-wt-Fc: KD = 16.2 ± 0.7 nM; ACE2-T92Q-Fc: KD = 8.0 ± 0.7 nM; ACE2-N322Q-Fc: KD = 11.4 ± 0.3 nM; Figure 6b; Figure 6—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is based on BLI measurements shown in Figure 6b.

claim: ACE2-wt-Fc has a KD of 16.2 ± 0.7 nM for RBD binding.
source: The BLI data are in good agreement with our computational models, confirming that the removal of protein N-glycosylation at either N90 or N322 results in up to twofold higher binding affinities, when compared to ACE2-wt-Fc (ACE2-wt-Fc: KD = 16.2 ± 0.7 nM; ACE2-T92Q-Fc: KD = 8.0 ± 0.7 nM; ACE2-N322Q-Fc: KD = 11.4 ± 0.3 nM; Figure 6b; Figure 6—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is based on BLI measurements shown in Figure 6b.

claim: Co-incubation of cells with SARS-CoV-2 and ACE2-T92Q-Fc resulted in significant further reduction of the viral load when compared to ACE2-wt-Fc.
source: Importantly, co-incubation of cells with SARS-CoV-2 and ACE2-T92Q-Fc resulted in significant further reduction of the viral load when compared to ACE2-wt-Fc.
evidence: This is based on virus neutralization assays shown in Figure 7.

claim: Enhanced SARS-CoV-2 neutralization was also observed for ACE2-N322Q-Fc.
source: Enhanced SARS-CoV-2 neutralization was also observed for ACE2-N322Q-Fc. However, this mutant was less effective in promoting virus neutralization than ACE2-T92Q-Fc (Figure 7 and Figure 7—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is based on virus neutralization assays shown in Figure 7 and Figure 7—figure supplement 1.

claim: ACE2-N322Q-Fc was less effective in promoting virus neutralization than ACE2-T92Q-Fc.
source: Enhanced SARS-CoV-2 neutralization was also observed for ACE2-N322Q-Fc. However, this mutant was less effective in promoting virus neutralization than ACE2-T92Q-Fc (Figure 7 and Figure 7—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is based on virus neutralization assays shown in Figure 7 and Figure 7—figure supplement 1.

claim: ACE2-T92Q-N322Q-Fc has a KD of 8.2 ± 0.2 nM for RBD binding.
source: Studies of the interaction between ACE2-T92Q-N322Q-Fc and deglyco-ACE2-wt-Fc with RBD by BLI analysis yielded KD values similar to those determined for the single mutant ACE2-T92Q-Fc (ACE2-T92Q-N322Q-Fc: KD = 8.2 ± 0.2 nM; deglyco-ACE2-wt-Fc: KD = 7.6 ± 0.3 nM).
evidence: This is based on BLI measurements shown in Figure 6b.

claim: Deglyco-ACE2-wt-Fc has a KD of 7.6 ± 0.3 nM for RBD binding.
source: Studies of the interaction between ACE2-T92Q-N322Q-Fc and deglyco-ACE2-wt-Fc with RBD by BLI analysis yielded KD values similar to those determined for the single mutant ACE2-T92Q-Fc (ACE2-T92Q-N322Q-Fc: KD = 8.2 ± 0.2 nM; deglyco-ACE2-wt-Fc: KD = 7.6 ± 0.3 nM).
evidence: This is based on BLI measurements shown in Figure 6b.

claim: Desialo-ACE2-wt-Fc has a KD of 11.3 ± 0.4 nM for RBD binding.
source: The affinity of desialo-ACE2-wt-Fc for RBD (KD = 11.3 ± 0.4 nM) was also higher than that of native ACE2-wt-Fc (Figure 6b).
evidence: This is based on BLI measurements shown in Figure 6b.

claim: The affinity of desialo-ACE2-wt-Fc for RBD was higher than that of native ACE2-wt-Fc.
source: The affinity of desialo-ACE2-wt-Fc for RBD (KD = 11.3 ± 0.4 nM) was also higher than that of native ACE2-wt-Fc (Figure 6b).
evidence: This is based on BLI measurements shown in Figure 6b.

claim: Deglyco-ACE2-wt-Fc followed by ACE2-T92Q-N322Q-Fc display the highest neutralization potencies.
source: The increased affinities of these ACE2-Fc variants for Spike correlate with their potencies to neutralize SARS-CoV-2, with deglyco-ACE2-wt-Fc followed by ACE2-T92Q-N322Q-Fc displaying the highest neutralization potencies (Figure 7 and Figure 7—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is based on virus neutralization assays shown in Figure 7 and Figure 7—figure supplement 2.

claim: The effect of desialo-ACE2-wt-Fc on SARS-CoV-2 infections of Vero E6 cells was less pronounced and comparable to that of the single mutant ACE2-N322Q-Fc.
source: The effect of desialo-ACE2-wt-Fc on SARS-CoV-2 infections of Vero E6 cells was less pronounced and comparable to that of the single mutant ACE2-N322Q-Fc (Figure 7), in good agreement with the almost identical RBD-binding affinities of these two ACE2-Fc variants (Figure 6b).
evidence: This is based on virus neutralization assays (Figure 7) and binding affinity measurements (Figure 6b).

claim: The binding affinity of deglyco-rshACE2 to RBD (KD = 5.1 ± 0.5 nM) is two times higher than for native rshACE2 (KD = 10.5 ± 0.4 nM).
source: Paralleling our observations with deglyco-ACE2-wt-Fc, we found the binding affinity of deglyco-rshACE2 to RBD (KD = 5.1 ± 0.5 nM) to be two times higher than for native rshACE2 (KD = 10.5 ± 0.4 nM; Figure 6b).
evidence: This is based on BLI measurements shown in Figure 6b.

claim: Deglyco-rshACE2 displayed improved SARS-CoV-2 neutralization properties in Vero E6 cell infection assays.
source: Furthermore, deglyco-rshACE2 displayed improved SARS-CoV-2 neutralization properties in Vero E6 cell infection assays.
evidence: This is based on virus neutralization assays shown in Figure 8.

claim: At a final concentration of 200 µg/mL deglyco-rshACE2, a significant reduction in SARS-CoV-2 replication was observed when compared to treatment with the native form of the protein.
source: At a final concentration of 200 µg/mL deglyco-rshACE2, we observed a significant reduction in SARS-CoV-2 replication when compared to treatment with the native form of the protein (Figure 8).
evidence: This is based on virus neutralization assays shown in Figure 8.

claim: The catalytic activities of ACE2-T92Q-Fc, ACE2-N322Q-Fc and ACE2-T92Q-N322Q-Fc were found to be only modestly reduced as compared to ACE2-wt-Fc.
source: In contrast to other recently described ACE2 mutants displaying improved Spike binding concomitant with inadvertently or intentionally impaired enzymatic activity (Glasgow et al., 2020; Chan et al., 2020), the catalytic activities of ACE2-T92Q-Fc, ACE2-N322Q-Fc and ACE2-T92Q-N322Q-Fc were found to be only modestly reduced as compared to ACE2-wt-Fc (ACE2-T92Q-Fc: 65% ± 11%; ACE2-N322Q-Fc: 69% ± 7%; ACE2-T92Q-N322Q-Fc: 79% ± 11%; Figure 9).
evidence: This is based on enzymatic activity assays shown in Figure 9.

claim: ACE2-T92Q-Fc retains 65% ± 11% of the catalytic activity of ACE2-wt-Fc.
source: In contrast to other recently described ACE2 mutants displaying improved Spike binding concomitant with inadvertently or intentionally impaired enzymatic activity (Glasgow et al., 2020; Chan et al., 2020), the catalytic activities of ACE2-T92Q-Fc, ACE2-N322Q-Fc and ACE2-T92Q-N322Q-Fc were found to be only modestly reduced as compared to ACE2-wt-Fc (ACE2-T92Q-Fc: 65% ± 11%; ACE2-N322Q-Fc: 69% ± 7%; ACE2-T92Q-N322Q-Fc: 79% ± 11%; Figure 9).
evidence: This is based on enzymatic activity assays shown in Figure 9.

claim: ACE2-N322Q-Fc retains 69% ± 7% of the catalytic activity of ACE2-wt-Fc.
source: In contrast to other recently described ACE2 mutants displaying improved Spike binding concomitant with inadvertently or intentionally impaired enzymatic activity (Glasgow et al., 2020; Chan et al., 2020), the catalytic activities of ACE2-T92Q-Fc, ACE2-N322Q-Fc and ACE2-T92Q-N322Q-Fc were found to be only modestly reduced as compared to ACE2-wt-Fc (ACE2-T92Q-Fc: 65% ± 11%; ACE2-N322Q-Fc: 69% ± 7%; ACE2-T92Q-N322Q-Fc: 79% ± 11%; Figure 9).
evidence: This is based on enzymatic activity assays shown in Figure 9.

claim: ACE2-T92Q-N322Q-Fc retains 79% ± 11% of the catalytic activity of ACE2-wt-Fc.
source: In contrast to other recently described ACE2 mutants displaying improved Spike binding concomitant with inadvertently or intentionally impaired enzymatic activity (Glasgow et al., 2020; Chan et al., 2020), the catalytic activities of ACE2-T92Q-Fc, ACE2-N322Q-Fc and ACE2-T92Q-N322Q-Fc were found to be only modestly reduced as compared to ACE2-wt-Fc (ACE2-T92Q-Fc: 65% ± 11%; ACE2-N322Q-Fc: 69% ± 7%; ACE2-T92Q-N322Q-Fc: 79% ± 11%; Figure 9).
evidence: This is based on enzymatic activity assays shown in Figure 9.

claim: Deglyco-ACE2-wt-Fc exhibits 149% ± 1% of the enzymatic activity of native ACE2-wt-Fc.
source: Interestingly, deglyco-ACE2-wt-Fc (149% ± 1 %) and desialo-ACE2-wt-Fc (160% ± 2 %) exhibited higher enzymatic activities than native ACE2-wt-Fc (Figure 10 and Figure 10—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is based on enzymatic activity assays shown in Figure 10 and Figure 10—figure supplement 1.

claim: Desialo-ACE2-wt-Fc exhibits 160% ± 2% of the enzymatic activity of native ACE2-wt-Fc.
source: Interestingly, deglyco-ACE2-wt-Fc (149% ± 1 %) and desialo-ACE2-wt-Fc (160% ± 2 %) exhibited higher enzymatic activities than native ACE2-wt-Fc (Figure 10 and Figure 10—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is based on enzymatic activity assays shown in Figure 10 and Figure 10—figure supplement 1.

claim: Deglyco-rshACE2 exhibits 113% ± 2% of the enzymatic activity of native rshACE2.
source: A similar observation was made for deglyco-rshACE2, although the enhancing effects of enzymatic deglycosylation on catalytic efficiency were less pronounced (113% ± 2% as compared to native rshACE2; Figure 10).
evidence: This is based on enzymatic activity assays shown in Figure 10.

claim: Enzymatic removal of N-glycans from ACE2-Fc and clinical-grade rshACE2 results in increased Spike binding.
source: These results show that enzymatic removal of N-glycans from ACE2-Fc and clinical-grade rshACE2 results in increased Spike binding and enhanced SARS-CoV-2 neutralization while preserving its potentially critical enzymatic activity.
evidence: This is supported by binding affinity data (Figure 6) and neutralization assays (Figures 7 and 8).

claim: Enzymatic removal of N-glycans from ACE2-Fc and clinical-grade rshACE2 results in enhanced SARS-CoV-2 neutralization.
source: These results show that enzymatic removal of N-glycans from ACE2-Fc and clinical-grade rshACE2 results in increased Spike binding and enhanced SARS-CoV-2 neutralization while preserving its potentially critical enzymatic activity.
evidence: This is supported by neutralization assays shown in Figures 7 and 8.

claim: Enzymatic removal of N-glycans from ACE2-Fc and clinical-grade rshACE2 preserves its potentially critical enzymatic activity.
source: These results show that enzymatic removal of N-glycans from ACE2-Fc and clinical-grade rshACE2 results in increased Spike binding and enhanced SARS-CoV-2 neutralization while preserving its potentially critical enzymatic activity.
evidence: This is supported by enzymatic activity assays shown in Figures 9 and 10.

claim: Glycans shield about 38% of the protein surface of Spike.
source: The average accessible area of protein atoms for non-glycosylated and glycosylated Spike was 1395 nm² and 864 nm², respectively, indicating that glycans shield about 38% of the protein surface of Spike, a value that is comparable to what was previously found in simulations of Spike alone (Sikora et al., 2021; Grant et al., 2020).
evidence: This is based on SASA calculations from MD simulations and corroborated by citations to previous work (Sikora et al., 2021; Grant et al., 2020).

claim: The average accessible area of protein atoms for non-glycosylated Spike was 1395 nm².
source: The average accessible area of protein atoms for non-glycosylated and glycosylated Spike was 1395 nm² and 864 nm², respectively, indicating that glycans shield about 38% of the protein surface of Spike, a value that is comparable to what was previously found in simulations of Spike alone (Sikora et al., 2021; Grant et al., 2020).
evidence: This is based on SASA calculations from MD simulations.

claim: The average accessible area of protein atoms for glycosylated Spike was 864 nm².
source: The average accessible area of protein atoms for non-glycosylated and glycosylated Spike was 1395 nm² and 864 nm², respectively, indicating that glycans shield about 38% of the protein surface of Spike, a value that is comparable to what was previously found in simulations of Spike alone (Sikora et al., 2021; Grant et al., 2020).
evidence: This is based on SASA calculations from MD simulations.

claim: The total interface area between Spike and ACE2 was 24.6 nm².
source: The total interface area was 24.6 nm², with glycans accounting for up to 51% of the interface area, that is 12.6 nm², contributed by the four most relevant glycans at positions N53, N90, N322, and N546 of ACE2 (Figure 3).
evidence: This is based on interface area calculations from MD simulations.

claim: Recombinant soluble human ACE2 (rshACE2) has been shown to bind Spike.
source: Recombinant soluble human ACE2 (rshACE2) has been shown to bind Spike (Wang et al., 2020), can effectively neutralize SARS-CoV-2 infections (Monteil et al., 2020, Monteil et al., 2021), and the corresponding drug candidate APN01 has undergone a phase II clinical trial for the treatment of hospitalized cases of COVID-19 (ClinicalTrials.gov Identifier: NCT04335136).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to published work (Wang et al., 2020).

claim: Recombinant soluble human ACE2 can effectively neutralize SARS-CoV-2 infections.
source: Recombinant soluble human ACE2 (rshACE2) has been shown to bind Spike (Wang et al., 2020), can effectively neutralize SARS-CoV-2 infections (Monteil et al., 2020, Monteil et al., 2021), and the corresponding drug candidate APN01 has undergone a phase II clinical trial for the treatment of hospitalized cases of COVID-19 (ClinicalTrials.gov Identifier: NCT04335136).
evidence: This is supported by citations to published work (Monteil et al., 2020, Monteil et al., 2021).

claim: The drug candidate APN01 has undergone a phase II clinical trial for the treatment of hospitalized cases of COVID-19.
source: Recombinant soluble human ACE2 (rshACE2) has been shown to bind Spike (Wang et al., 2020), can effectively neutralize SARS-CoV-2 infections (Monteil et al., 2020, Monteil et al., 2021), and the corresponding drug candidate APN01 has undergone a phase II clinical trial for the treatment of hospitalized cases of COVID-19 (ClinicalTrials.gov Identifier: NCT04335136).
evidence: This is supported by reference to a clinical trial identifier (ClinicalTrials.gov Identifier: NCT04335136).

claim: A first case study of APN01 use in a patient has been reported recently.
source: A first case study of its use in a patient has been reported recently (Zoufaly et al., 2020).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to published work (Zoufaly et al., 2020).

claim: An aerosol formulation of APN01 has been developed and is currently undergoing Phase I clinical studies.
source: Additionally, an aerosol formulation of APN01 has been developed and is currently undergoing Phase I clinical studies.
evidence: This is stated as a fact in the Introduction section.

claim: Using soluble ACE2 as a decoy receptor for Spike is particularly attractive, as it minimizes the risk that variants of concern may evade the treatment through mutations as has been observed for antibodies.
source: Using soluble ACE2 as a decoy receptor for Spike is particularly attractive, as it minimizes the risk that variants of concern may evade the treatment through mutations as has been observed for antibodies (Weisblum et al., 2020; Li et al., 2021; Yuan et al., 2021).
evidence: This is supported by citations to published work on antibody escape (Weisblum et al., 2020; Li et al., 2021; Yuan et al., 2021).

claim: Protein engineering has yielded ACE2 variants with substantially improved affinities for Spike.
source: Furthermore, protein engineering has yielded ACE2 variants with substantially improved affinities for Spike (Glasgow et al., 2020; Chan et al., 2020).
evidence: This is supported by citations to published work (Glasgow et al., 2020; Chan et al., 2020).

claim: Soluble ACE2-based therapeutics offer considerable advantages over other therapeutic formats that aim to hamper the Spike-ACE2 interaction sterically.
source: Hence, soluble ACE2-based therapeutics offer considerable advantages over other therapeutic formats that aim to hamper the Spike-ACE2 interaction sterically.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the discussion of escape mutations and improved ACE2 variants.

claim: Structures of the complex between ACE2 and the receptor binding domain (RBD) were solved by X-ray crystallography or cryo-electron microscopy within 3 months after identification of SARS-CoV-2.
source: A mere 3 months after identification of SARS-CoV-2 as the etiologic agent of COVID-19, structures of the complex between ACE2 and the receptor binding domain (RBD) (Wang et al., 2020; Lan et al., 2020; Yan et al., 2020) and of the ectodomain of trimeric Spike (Walls et al., 2020; Wrapp et al., 2020) were already solved by X-ray crystallography or cryo-electron microscopy.
evidence: This is supported by citations to published structural studies (Wang et al., 2020; Lan et al., 2020; Yan et al., 2020; Walls et al., 2020; Wrapp et al., 2020).

claim: Structures of the ectodomain of trimeric Spike were solved by X-ray crystallography or cryo-electron microscopy within 3 months after identification of SARS-CoV-2.
source: A mere 3 months after identification of SARS-CoV-2 as the etiologic agent of COVID-19, structures of the complex between ACE2 and the receptor binding domain (RBD) (Wang et al., 2020; Lan et al., 2020; Yan et al., 2020) and of the ectodomain of trimeric Spike (Walls et al., 2020; Wrapp et al., 2020) were already solved by X-ray crystallography or cryo-electron microscopy.
evidence: This is supported by citations to published structural studies (Walls et al., 2020; Wrapp et al., 2020).

claim: The structural impact of protein-bound glycans on the Spike-ACE2 interface could not be assessed experimentally so far due to their compositional diversity and conformational flexibility.
source: While this provided unprecedented insight into the protein-protein interactions between Spike and ACE2, the structural impact of protein-bound glycans on the Spike-ACE2 interface could not be assessed experimentally so far due to their compositional diversity and conformational flexibility.
evidence: This is stated as a limitation of experimental structural biology and provides justification for the computational approach.

claim: In silico modeling of the glycans offers a powerful alternative to study the effects of individual Spike and ACE2 glycans on the molecular interactions between these two proteins.
source: Here, in silico modeling of the glycans offers a powerful alternative to study the effects of individual Spike and ACE2 glycans on the molecular interactions between these two proteins.
evidence: This is stated as the rationale for the computational approach taken in this study.

claim: Extensive all-atom molecular dynamics (MD) simulations indicated that Spike N-glycans attached to N165 and N234 could be important stabilizers of the ligand-accessible conformation of the receptor binding domain (RBD).
source: Extensive all-atom molecular dynamics (MD) simulations indicated that Spike N-glycans attached to N165 and N234 could be important stabilizers of the ligand-accessible conformation of the receptor binding domain (RBD) (Casalino et al., 2020).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to published MD simulation work (Casalino et al., 2020).

claim: It has been proposed that the N-glycan at position N343 acts as a gate facilitating RBD opening.
source: Furthermore, it has been proposed that the N-glycan at position N343 acts as a gate facilitating RBD opening (Sztain et al., 2021).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to published work (Sztain et al., 2021).

claim: Other MD studies concluded that the glycans attached to N90 and N322 of ACE2 could be major determinants of Spike binding.
source: Other MD studies concluded that the glycans attached to N90 and N322 of ACE2 could be major determinants of Spike binding (Mehdipour and Hummer, 2021), while yet other simulation works postulate that glycosylation does not affect the RBD-ACE2 interaction significantly (Cong et al., 2021; Delgado et al., 2021).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to published MD simulation work (Mehdipour and Hummer, 2021).

claim: Some simulation works postulate that glycosylation does not affect the RBD-ACE2 interaction significantly.
source: Other MD studies concluded that the glycans attached to N90 and N322 of ACE2 could be major determinants of Spike binding (Mehdipour and Hummer, 2021), while yet other simulation works postulate that glycosylation does not affect the RBD-ACE2 interaction significantly (Cong et al., 2021; Delgado et al., 2021).
evidence: This is supported by citations to published simulation work (Cong et al., 2021; Delgado et al., 2021).

claim: Genetic or pharmacological blockade of N-glycan biosynthesis at the oligomannose stage in ACE2-expressing target cells was found to dramatically reduce viral entry.
source: Genetic or pharmacological blockade of N-glycan biosynthesis at the oligomannose stage in ACE2-expressing target cells was found to dramatically reduce viral entry (Yang et al., 2020), even though several glycoforms of ACE2 were found to display comparatively moderate variation with respect to Spike binding (Allen et al., 2021).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to published work (Yang et al., 2020).

claim: Several glycoforms of ACE2 were found to display comparatively moderate variation with respect to Spike binding.
source: Genetic or pharmacological blockade of N-glycan biosynthesis at the oligomannose stage in ACE2-expressing target cells was found to dramatically reduce viral entry (Yang et al., 2020), even though several glycoforms of ACE2 were found to display comparatively moderate variation with respect to Spike binding (Allen et al., 2021).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to published work (Allen et al., 2021).

claim: The RBD of Spike exists in two distinct conformations, referred to as 'up' and 'down'.
source: The RBD of Spike exists in two distinct conformations, referred to as 'up' and 'down' (Walls et al., 2020; Wrapp et al., 2020).
evidence: This is supported by citations to published structural studies (Walls et al., 2020; Wrapp et al., 2020).

claim: The 'up' conformation corresponds to the receptor-accessible state with the RBD of one monomer exposed.
source: The 'up' conformation corresponds to the receptor-accessible state with the RBD of one monomer exposed.
evidence: This is based on established knowledge from structural studies of Spike.

claim: Cryo-EM structures with more than one RBD in the 'up' conformation were shown to bind to two separate hACE2 molecules (rather than one single hACE2 dimer).
source: Of note, although cryo-EM structures with more than one RBD in the 'up' conformation were shown to bind to two separate hACE2 molecules (rather than one single hACE2 dimer) (Benton et al., 2020), we decided to study the effect of the glycans on the Spike hACE2 interaction using the model with a single RBD in the 'up' conformation.
evidence: This is supported by a citation to published structural work (Benton et al., 2020).

claim: The glycome of rshACE2 was elucidated, providing information on the glycans attached to N690, a glycosylation site not covered in previous glycoproteomic studies of soluble hACE2.
source: To assess the impact of all seven individual N-glycosylation sites of hACE2 on its interaction with Spike, we first elucidated the entire glycome of rshACE2 (Figure 1—figure supplement 1). This also provided information on the glycans attached to N690, a glycosylation site not covered in previous glycoproteomic studies of soluble hACE2 (Zhao et al., 2020; Allen et al., 2021).
evidence: This is based on the authors' own glycoproteomic analysis shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: The glyco-analysis of recombinant trimeric Spike has been reported elsewhere.
source: For recombinant trimeric Spike, the glyco-analysis has been reported elsewhere (Hoffmann et al., 2021; Watanabe et al., 2020; Zhao et al., 2020; Sun et al., 2021).
evidence: This is supported by citations to published glycoproteomic studies (Hoffmann et al., 2021; Watanabe et al., 2020; Zhao et al., 2020; Sun et al., 2021).

claim: Fully glycosylated atomistic models of the trimeric Spike glycoprotein, free dimeric ACE2 and of the Spike glycoprotein in complex with dimeric hACE2 were constructed.
source: We hence constructed fully glycosylated atomistic models of the trimeric Spike glycoprotein, free dimeric ACE2 and of the Spike glycoprotein in complex with dimeric hACE2 (Figure 1).
evidence: This is stated as a methodological step and shown in Figure 1.

claim: Molecular dynamics simulations of the Spike-ACE2 complex and of free hACE2 were performed.
source: As glycans are known to be particularly flexible, and these were modeled in a single low-energy conformation, we subsequently performed molecular dynamics simulations of the Spike-ACE2 complex (Video 1), and of free hACE2.
evidence: This is stated as a methodological step and illustrated in Video 1.

claim: Enzymatic desialylation of ACE2 results in a reproducible increase of its affinity to RBD without detectable structural penalties.
source: It has been reported that the sialylation status of ACE2 affects its interactions with SARS-CoV-2 Spike (Allen et al., 2021). We have found that enzymatic desialylation of ACE2 results in a reproducible increase of its affinity to RBD without detectable structural penalties.
evidence: This is based on the authors' BLI measurements (Figure 6b) and DSC data (Figure 5).

claim: Desialylated ACE2 is more efficient in neutralizing SARS-CoV-2 than its native counterpart.
source: Importantly, desialylated ACE2 is more efficient in neutralizing SARS-CoV-2 than its native counterpart.
evidence: This is based on virus neutralization assays shown in Figure 7.

claim: Molecular simulations suggest that the terminal sialic acids of the N-glycans attached to ACE2 residues N90 and N322 mask parts of the Spike-ACE2 interface.
source: Molecular simulations suggest that the terminal sialic acids of the N-glycans attached to ACE2 residues N90 and N322 mask parts of the Spike-ACE2 interface and thus could interfere with Spike binding through steric clashes and/or electrostatic effects (Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is based on density map analysis from MD simulations shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1.

claim: Terminal sialic acids on ACE2 N-glycans could interfere with Spike binding through steric clashes and/or electrostatic effects.
source: Molecular simulations suggest that the terminal sialic acids of the N-glycans attached to ACE2 residues N90 and N322 mask parts of the Spike-ACE2 interface and thus could interfere with Spike binding through steric clashes and/or electrostatic effects (Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is a speculation based on the MD simulation data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1.

claim: Sialic acids present on ACE2 might dampen interactions with Spike during SARS-CoV-2 attachment to host cells.
source: This provides a structural rationale how sialic acids present on ACE2 might dampen interactions with Spike during SARS-CoV-2 attachment to host cells (Chu et al., 2021).
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the MD simulation data and supported by a citation (Chu et al., 2021).

claim: Elimination of the N-glycans attached to N90 is largely responsible for the improved Spike-binding properties of enzymatically deglycosylated ACE2.
source: In line with other reports (Chan et al., 2020; Chu et al., 2021), our results indicate that the elimination of the N-glycans attached to N90 is largely responsible for the improved Spike-binding properties of enzymatically deglycosylated ACE2.
evidence: This is based on the authors' binding affinity data (Figure 6) and supported by citations to other reports (Chan et al., 2020; Chu et al., 2021).

claim: Substitution of ACE2 residues N90 or T92 could provide an alternative approach for the development of ACE2 variants with improved SARS-CoV-2 sequestering properties.
source: As proposed (Glasgow et al., 2020; Chan et al., 2020) and corroborated by our mutational analysis, substitution of ACE2 residues N90 or T92 could indeed provide an alternative approach for the development of ACE2 variants with improved SARS-CoV-2 sequestering properties.
evidence: This is based on the authors' mutational analysis data (Figures 6 and 7) and supported by citations to previous proposals (Glasgow et al., 2020; Chan et al., 2020).

claim: Ablation of N90 glycosylation could be combined with mutations of N322 and possibly other ACE2 N-glycosylation sites to achieve an even higher SARS-CoV-2 neutralizing potency.
source: Our data indicate that ablation of N90 glycosylation could be combined with mutations of N322 and possibly other ACE2 N-glycosylation sites to achieve an even higher SARS-CoV-2 neutralizing potency.
evidence: This is a speculation based on the authors' data showing additive effects of N90 and N322 mutations (Figures 6 and 7).

claim: Expression of an ACE2 variant lacking all potential N-glycosylation sites in ACE2-negative host cells led to reduced rather than enhanced susceptibility of the cells to SARS-CoV-2 as compared to transduction with wild-type ACE2.
source: However, expression of an ACE2 variant lacking all potential N-glycosylation sites in ACE2-negative host cells led to reduced rather than enhanced susceptibility of the cells to SARS-CoV-2 as compared to transduction with wild-type ACE2 (Chu et al., 2021).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to published work (Chu et al., 2021).

claim: The much lower cellular content of the glycan-free ACE2 mutant relative to the native enzyme demonstrates that the importance of N-glycosylation for proper folding of glycoproteins during their biosynthesis also applies to ACE2.
source: This was attributed to the much lower cellular content of the mutant protein relative to the native enzyme, thus demonstrating that the importance of N-glycosylation for proper folding of glycoproteins during their biosynthesis (Xu and Ng, 2015) also applies to ACE2.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the cited observation and supported by a citation on glycoprotein folding (Xu and Ng, 2015).

claim: The clinical potential of enzymatically deglycosylated rshACE2 is superior to that of any ACE2 glycomutants.
source: Given the inferior expression yields of glycan-free ACE2 and the potential of unwanted immunological side effects when non-natural mutations are introduced into a therapeutic glycoprotein, we believe that the clinical potential of enzymatically deglycosylated rshACE2 is superior to that of any of our ACE2 glycomutants.
evidence: This is an opinion/speculation based on the authors' consideration of expression yields and immunological concerns.

claim: Treatment of clinical-grade rshACE2 with deglycosylation enzymes such as PNGase F followed by a final polishing step represents a straightforward, Good Manufacturing Practice (GMP)-compliant and industrially feasible alternative to generate a potent therapeutic drug for the treatment of SARS-CoV-2 infected persons and patients.
source: In our opinion, treatment of clinical-grade rshACE2 with deglycosylation enzymes such as PNGase F followed by a final polishing step represents a straightforward, Good Manufacturing Practice (GMP)-compliant and industrially feasible alternative to generate a potent therapeutic drug for the treatment of SARS-CoV-2 infected persons and patients.
evidence: This is an opinion/speculation based on the authors' experimental results and consideration of manufacturing feasibility.

claim: Structure-guided glycoengineering is a powerful means to develop ACE2 variants with improved SARS-CoV-2 neutralization properties without compromising the structural stability and catalytic activity of the enzyme.
source: Our data demonstrate that structure-guided glycoengineering is a powerful means to develop ACE2 variants with improved SARS-CoV-2 neutralization properties without compromising the structural stability and catalytic activity of the enzyme.
evidence: This is a summary conclusion supported by the combined data from MD simulations, binding assays, neutralization assays, DSC, and enzymatic activity measurements presented throughout the manuscript.

claim: In silico models of the Spike-ACE2 complex combined with simulations of its spatial and temporal dynamics rationalized previously published data.
source: Our in silico models of the Spike-ACE2 complex combined with simulations of its spatial and temporal dynamics rationalized previously published data and led to predictions that were confirmed by in vitro binding studies and cell-based SARS-CoV-2 neutralization assays.
evidence: This is supported by the agreement between the authors' MD simulation results and previously published experimental findings cited throughout the manuscript.

claim: In silico models led to predictions that were confirmed by in vitro binding studies and cell-based SARS-CoV-2 neutralization assays.
source: Our in silico models of the Spike-ACE2 complex combined with simulations of its spatial and temporal dynamics rationalized previously published data and led to predictions that were confirmed by in vitro binding studies and cell-based SARS-CoV-2 neutralization assays.
evidence: This is supported by the experimental validation of the computational predictions shown in Figures 6, 7, and 8.

claim: A cooperative effect may be expected for the association of trimeric Spike molecules present in the viral envelope with ACE2 dimers.
source: Second, a cooperative effect may be expected for the association of trimeric Spike molecules present in the viral envelope with ACE2 dimers. In this supramolecular setting, a subtle increase in the affinity of ACE2 for RBD can lead to a dynamic equilibrium of binding and unbinding events with up to six potential interactions, leading to an overall much stronger avidity effect.
evidence: This is a speculation/inference to explain the discrepancy between modest affinity improvements and larger neutralization effects.

claim: In the supramolecular setting of trimeric Spike and dimeric ACE2, a subtle increase in the affinity of ACE2 for RBD can lead to a dynamic equilibrium of binding and unbinding events with up to six potential interactions, leading to an overall much stronger avidity effect.
source: Second, a cooperative effect may be expected for the association of trimeric Spike molecules present in the viral envelope with ACE2 dimers. In this supramolecular setting, a subtle increase in the affinity of ACE2 for RBD can lead to a dynamic equilibrium of binding and unbinding events with up to six potential interactions, leading to an overall much stronger avidity effect.
evidence: This is a speculation/inference based on the multivalent nature of the Spike-ACE2 interaction.

claim: The dynamic equilibrium of the RBDs between 'down' and 'up' conformations can further steepen the dose-response curves.
source: The dynamic equilibrium of the RBDs between 'down' and 'up' conformations can further steepen the dose-response curves (Monod et al., 1965).
evidence: This is an inference supported by a citation to a classic paper on cooperative binding (Monod et al., 1965).

claim: A slight advantage of the soluble ACE2 decoy receptor over endogenous native ACE2 may be sufficient to tip the balance between SARS-CoV-2 attachment and shedding of viral particles from the host cell surface.
source: Third, a slight advantage of the soluble ACE2 decoy receptor over endogenous native ACE2 may be sufficient to tip the balance between SARS-CoV-2 attachment and shedding of viral particles from the host cell surface. The inhibitory strength is not a function of the number of Spike proteins that are bound, but of the probability that a high enough fraction of Spike proteins is bound, potentiating a small increase in affinity (Magnus, 2013).
evidence: This is a speculation/inference supported by a citation (Magnus, 2013).

claim: The SARS-CoV-2 neutralization assays shown in Figure 7 were performed at a low multiplicity of infection.
source: Fourth, the SARS-CoV-2 neutralization assays shown in Figure 7 were performed at a low multiplicity of infection. This can lead to complete neutralization of all virus particles in the inoculum (Monteil et al., 2020) as becomes evident from the individual data points of our experiments (Figure 7—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is stated as a methodological detail and shown in the data (Figure 7 and Figure 7—figure supplement 1).

claim: Low multiplicity of infection can lead to complete neutralization of all virus particles in the inoculum.
source: Fourth, the SARS-CoV-2 neutralization assays shown in Figure 7 were performed at a low multiplicity of infection. This can lead to complete neutralization of all virus particles in the inoculum (Monteil et al., 2020) as becomes evident from the individual data points of our experiments (Figure 7—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by a citation (Monteil et al., 2020) and the authors' own data (Figure 7—figure supplement 1).

claim: It is possible that the N-glycan moiety of ACE2 also modulates other aspects of viral entry besides promoting the docking of Spike to the cell surface.
source: Finally, it is possible that the N-glycan moiety of ACE2 also modulates other aspects of viral entry besides promoting the docking of Spike to the cell surface (Yang et al., 2020).
evidence: This is a speculation supported by a citation (Yang et al., 2020).

claim: All virus-neutralization experiments presented in this paper were performed using Vero E6 cells.
source: We want to point out that all virus-neutralization experiments presented in this paper were performed using Vero E6 cells.
evidence: This is stated as a methodological detail in the Discussion section.

claim: It will be important to repeat the neutralization assays with a cell line derived from human lung (e.g. Calu-3).
source: Although this cell line is very popular for SARS-CoV-2 propagation and infectivity studies, it will be important to repeat our neutralization assays with a cell line derived from human lung (e.g. Calu-3) (Johnson et al., 2021).
evidence: This is stated as a future direction/limitation and supported by a citation (Johnson et al., 2021).

claim: Native ACE2 does not display any cytotoxic effects even when used at very high concentrations.
source: However, we have shown previously that native ACE2 does not display any cytotoxic effects even when used at very high concentrations (Monteil et al., 2020).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to the authors' previous work (Monteil et al., 2020).

claim: rshACE2 regulates blood pressure and protects multiple organs such as the heart, kidney and lung as well as blood vessels via enzymatic degradation of angiotensin II.
source: Besides serving as a soluble decoy receptor to prevent SARS-CoV-2 infection of ACE2-expressing host cells, rshACE2 also regulates blood pressure and protects multiple organs such as the heart, kidney and lung as well as blood vessels via enzymatic degradation of angiotensin II (Vickers et al., 2002).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to published work (Vickers et al., 2002).

claim: Other recently described ACE2 mutants display improved Spike binding concomitant with inadvertently or intentionally impaired enzymatic activity.
source: In contrast to other recently described ACE2 mutants displaying improved Spike binding concomitant with inadvertently or intentionally impaired enzymatic activity (Glasgow et al., 2020; Chan et al., 2020), the catalytic activities of ACE2-T92Q-Fc, ACE2-N322Q-Fc and ACE2-T92Q-N322Q-Fc were found to be only modestly reduced as compared to ACE2-wt-Fc (ACE2-T92Q-Fc: 65% ± 11%; ACE2-N322Q-Fc: 69% ± 7%; ACE2-T92Q-N322Q-Fc: 79% ± 11%; Figure 9).
evidence: This is supported by citations to published work (Glasgow et al., 2020; Chan et al., 2020).
